content: The studies included in this analysis were limited to those using whole blood, plasma, or serum samples, and only studies that examined at least 10 independent HCV NAT-positive samples were considered. Saliva specimens were also reviewed, but only one study was identified, which did not use NAT as a reference test and was therefore excluded. Commercially prepared reference panel specimens were also excluded. Studies that utilized commercially available HCV Core Antigen (HCV cAg) tests were eligible for inclusion. Acute HCV infection was defined as the six-month period following the acquisition of the hepatitis C virus. During this time, HCV antibodies (HCV Ab) may be positive or negative, and the time between initial infection and antibody seroconversion is referred to as the window period. HCV RNA is detectable during this phase. Chronic HCV infection was defined as an infection lasting more than six months, during which both HCV Ab and RNA are detectable. For monitoring viral clearance during treatment, rapid viral response (RVR) at four weeks, early viral response (EVR) at 12 weeks, and sustained viral response (SVR) at 24 weeks post-treatment were assessed. The reference standards for definitive diagnosis included tests for HCV RNA detection using NAT techniques such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR), branched-chain DNA (bDNA), or transcription-mediated amplification (TMA). These tests were either qualitative or quantitative, and their performance characteristics were considered similar above 50 IU/mL. All NATs were treated as a single reference standard. Sensitivity was defined as the proportion of true HCV infections diagnosed with a positive HCV Core Ag test confirmed by a positive NAT result. Specificity referred to the proportion of samples with a negative HCV Core Ag test and no evidence of active HCV infection confirmed by a negative NAT result. A comprehensive database search of EMBASE, PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane was conducted through March 2015, with no language restrictions. Two independent reviewers assessed titles and abstracts to identify potentially eligible studies, and full-text articles were retrieved for further evaluation. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion or by a third reviewer. Studies were categorized based on their relevance to specific PICO questions, and reasons for exclusion were documented. Data extraction was performed using a standardized form, which was pilot-tested and finalized. Two reviewers independently extracted data, and disagreements were resolved through discussion or by a third reviewer. Authors of studies with incomplete data were contacted for additional information. Studies without extractable sensitivity and specificity data were excluded if no further information was obtained after three attempts to contact the authors. The methodological quality of included studies was assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool, a validated instrument for diagnostic studies. Statistical analyses were performed using STATA software, and studies were grouped by the type of index test used. Indeterminate test results were excluded from sensitivity and specificity analyses, as they accounted for less than 1% of all index tests. Publication bias was not formally assessed, as funnel plot asymmetry tests are not recommended for diagnostic test accuracy studies. Meta-analyses were conducted for index test types with at least four studies and ten independent samples per study. Bivariate random-effects meta-analyses were performed when sufficient data were available to calculate sensitivity, specificity, and 95% confidence intervals. For studies contributing data to only one metric (sensitivity or specificity), univariate random-effects meta-analyses were performed. Descriptive analyses were conducted for index tests with fewer than four studies or substantial heterogeneity. Heterogeneity among studies was visually assessed using forest plots and scatter plots of sensitivity versus 1-specificity. The variability in estimates and the width of prediction regions were examined, with wider prediction regions indicating greater heterogeneity. Between-study variability was quantified using τ². Subgroup analyses were pre-specified based on antibody status, specimen condition (fresh vs. frozen), HBV and HIV co-infection status, and genotype distribution. However, meta-regression to assess the impact of covariates was limited due to insufficient data. Outliers were identified, and descriptive statistics were performed. Only the Abbott ARCHITECT assay had sufficient quantitative data for analysis. From the literature search, 8,146 citations were identified, and 313 full-text articles were reviewed. Of these, 50 studies were included for PICO 5a, and four studies were included for PICO 9. The included studies utilized seven different HCV Core Ag assays, with the Abbott ARCHITECT HCV Ag assay being the most frequently assessed in 30 studies. Most studies were cross-sectional or cohort designs with broad study populations, except for one study that evaluated only healthy blood donors. The methodological quality of studies was generally high, with most studies judged to have a low risk of bias in patient selection, index test application, and reference standard use. However, some studies had unclear risks due to unspecified enrollment or prior exclusion strategies. Applicability concerns were minimal, as most studies included patients with active HCV infection. The pooled sensitivity and specificity estimates for the Abbott ARCHITECT assay demonstrated good accuracy for diagnosing HCV infection, with relatively homogeneous results across studies. However, heterogeneity was observed in some analyses, particularly for antibody-negative specimens. The Ortho ELISA-Ag test also showed good accuracy, though with some heterogeneity. Other assays, such as the Bio-Rad Monolisa HCV Ag-Ab ULTRA and EIKEN Lumispot HCV Ag, had limited data and substantial heterogeneity, precluding pooled analyses. Quantitative analyses revealed a strong correlation between HCV Core Ag and RNA levels, with sensitivity decreasing at lower RNA levels (<3,000 IU/mL). The Abbott ARCHITECT assay showed high sensitivity and specificity at baseline and during treatment monitoring, though data for predicting SVR were limited. In conclusion, HCV Core Ag assays, particularly the Abbott ARCHITECT, demonstrate good diagnostic accuracy for active HCV infection and may serve as a useful alternative to NAT in certain settings. However, further studies are needed to evaluate their performance in diverse populations and under varying clinical conditions.
